extracted.intended_audience: aspiring writers and prospective authors (contributors to periodicals and pamphlets)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for individuals deciding whether to write or publish: what qualifications, knowledge, style, motives, and preparatory practices mark someone fit to be an author. Emphasises subject-matter mastery, language mastery, study of models, and avoiding premature or arrogant publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper qualifications to write
rubrics_metrics.description: "He who has not obtained the proper qualifications of an author, can have no excuse for the arrogance of writing, but the power of imparting to mankind something necessary to be known."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only justify publishing when you can impart something necessary or genuinely useful; occasional useful revelations from the uneducated are possible but rare. Most books and pamphlets add little to real knowledge and merely transpose common sentiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfect knowledge of the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: "The first qualification of a writer is a perfect knowledge of the subject which he undertakes to treat; since we cannot teach what we do not know, nor can properly undertake to instruct others while we are ourselves in want of instruction."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before writing on a topic, read and compare the writers who have discussed it, familiarise their arguments by long meditation, consult the foundations of different systems, and separate truth from error by rigorous examination. Do not attempt to teach where you lack real understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of the language and appropriate style
rubrics_metrics.description: "The next requisite is, that he be master of the language in which he delivers his sentiments: if he treats of science and demonstration, that he has attained a style clear, pure, nervous, and expressive; if his topicks be probable and persuasory, that he be able to recommend them by the superaddition of elegance and imagery, to display the colours of varied diction, and pour forth the musick of modulated periods."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match style to purpose: clarity and precision for demonstration; elegance, imagery and varied diction for persuasion. Develop diction, cadence, and rhetorical figures to suit the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form style by studying the best models
rubrics_metrics.description: "He only has a right to suppose that he can express his thoughts ... who has carefully perused the best authors, accurately noted their diversities of style, diligently selected the best modes of diction, and familiarized them by long habits of attentive practice."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively read exemplary authors, note stylistic differences, select the most effective modes of diction, and internalise them through repeated practice. Style is formed, not accidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test your abilities before assuming competence
rubrics_metrics.description: "He only can rationally presume that he understands a subject, who has read and compared the writers that have hitherto discussed it, familiarized their arguments to himself by long meditation, consulted the foundations of different systems, and separated truth from errour by a rigorous examination."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparative reading, long meditation, and critical examination of foundations to test whether you truly understand a topic; mere inclination or superficial acquaintance is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid premature publication and arrogance
rubrics_metrics.description: "No man is a rhetorician or philosopher by chance... he that without forming his style by the study of the best models hastens to obtrude his compositions on the publick, may be certain... he shall shock the learned ear with barbarisms, and contribute... to the depravation of taste and the corruption of language."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rush to publish; premature or ill-formed works offend informed readers and degrade public taste. The anti-pattern is hastily obtruding unstudied compositions on the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient substance and confidence to publish
rubrics_metrics.description: "Some indeed there are, of both sexes, who are authors only in desire,... whose performances have not arrived at bulk sufficient to form a volume, or who have not the confidence... to solicit openly the assistance of the printer."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to produce performances of adequate bulk and quality before seeking publication; mere desire or occasional letters to periodicals are not the same as a considered body of work ready for printing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right motive: do not write solely for fame or patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay cautions that many write driven by "the itch of literary praise" and that one should "fix their thoughts upon some salutary considerations, which might repress their ardour for that reputation, which not one of many thousands is fated to obtain."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate motives: avoid writing merely for reputation, patronage, or riches. Prefer salutary aims (imparting useful knowledge, improving taste, beneficence) over pursuit of fame.
